messages.content:
While not directly related to any of the ongoing SAIR competitions, I just made public a project that falls in between several of the topics and used AI heavily, and I thought some people might be interested:

I'm happy to announce an explicit presentation for the absolute Galois group of of Q2\mathbb{Q}_2Q2​, with four generators and two relations (joint with David Turturean).  Details are available on our project website. This solves a 44-year-old problem I submitted to Epoch AI's open-problems list last winter. Of particular interest to this community:

We made heavy use of AI at all stages of the project. The presentations were found using Fable 5 and GPT; the proof was written using GPT-5.5-Pro (apparently a stealth 5.6; see David's account on the development page); we created two separate formalizations in Lean using Claude and GPT agents with human orchestration; and Fable did most of the website and paper revision. See our development page for more details.

After using AI so heavily in the first two parts of the project, I wanted to experiment with an AI-centered paper-writing process. I've tried to build this process into a separate project, PaperForge. The hope is that AI-written mathematics papers can be more readable than human ones eventually. Here are some ways that I think AI-written papers can add value for readers and authors.

  • One of the main benefits for authors is that the writing process can be faster since much of it is delegated to AI. Of course, this is true with AI slop as well. But the flip side is that if an author is willing to put in some work, AI can quickly build usability features that would be very annoying to do manually.
  • One such feature is differing levels of detail in exposition. PDF papers need to pick a target audience and stick with it; inspired by LMFDB knowls we've added expandable detail levels, allowing the paper to contain more detail on arguments that the reader can choose to expand or bypass.
  • Another is notation tooltips. Instead of having a big table of notation that you have to refer to, you can just hover over the symbol and see a popup with the definition (and a link to the location it was defined). This also applies for background material: an appendix summarizes background material, and whenever these terms appear there is a popup with a short explanation and link for more information.
  • The underlying data format is PreTeXt, though I think Typst is also a viable option (I chose PreTeXt mostly for maturity reasons).
  • The presence of a formalization also anchors AI writing, reducing the risk of hallucinated claims or citations. Having formalization show up inline as you read the paper is hopefully useful.
  • For more details see the PaperForge repo. It's still very preliminary (it's only been used on one project so far) but I'm happy to get feedback and welcome PRs.
